A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MTPC research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite the revised title and substantial reorganisation.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix D report original EvaByte experiments measuring acceptance, latency and throughput, including circuit-rank, prediction-window and LoRA ablations.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices K–L report original EvaByte and byte-level Llama experiments. Appendix F.1 also reports inference-memory measurements.

M1.justification: The FF, CP, inhomogeneous HMM and BTree architectures, likelihood-based training, LoRA layer sharing and decoding procedures remain substantively unchanged. Algorithms 1–3 are retained. The Llama experiments reuse this framework; Appendix G discusses possible future memory-saving adaptations rather than changes to the evaluated method.

E1.justification: Both versions fine-tune on the Tülu 3 SFT mix and evaluate generation on English validation prompts. Llama adds a model configuration, not new data or task coverage. The downstream benchmarks in v2 Table 4 are explicitly reproduced from EvaByte's authors rather than newly evaluated with MTPC.

E2.justification: The STP and fully factorised FF baselines remain, as do comparisons among CP, HMM and BTree. Added Llama and greedy-decoding results use these same comparison families. Hydra and EAGLE remain unevaluated, and the additional model names in v2 Table 4 belong to reproduced external results.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from EvaByte 6.5B to include Llama 3.2 3B Byte, with different model dimensions and no MTP pretraining. Section 4.2 revises stated throughput from mean accepted tokens divided by mean latency to total generated tokens divided by total generation latency, excluding prefill. New memory profiling specifies cached generation of 1,024 tokens. These establish expanded settings and a reported metric revision, without establishing which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The rank, window-size and LoRA analyses are expanded across backbones and reported decoding regimes, exposing when expressiveness helps. New Appendices C, F.1 and G analyse circuit/head computation, measured inference memory and vocabulary-dependent training-memory requirements. The earlier HMM-configuration and alternative-loss analyses remain in Appendices H and J.

E5.justification: Both versions describe three runs using different sets of 250 prompts, and L40S tables retain mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting. However, v2 Tables 19–20 omit the standard deviations present in the corresponding RTX 3090 results in v1 Tables 4–5. This is reduced uncertainty reporting; the PDFs do not establish fewer runs.

E6.justification: EvaByte results are revised throughout. For L40S sampling, the reported best configuration changes from BTree with n=16 and two LoRA layers at 219.1 tokens/s, 5.47× STP, to one layer at 203.1 tokens/s, 5.15× STP (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 9). New Llama results reach 87.7 tokens/s and 2.24× STP in Table 15. Greedy results also reveal FF outperforming expressive heads for EvaByte. These are revised and added results, not a controlled performance decline across versions given the changed metric definition.

T1.justification: The circuit factorisations, smoothness/decomposability definition and tractability arguments are retained. Appendices D and G add explicit memory-scaling arguments, including O(nsd) versus O(sd) feature storage and snvr logit storage, together with a possible low-rank unembedding parameterisation. No substantial new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain expressive circuit-based MTP, expressiveness–latency trade-offs and preservation of verifier quality. The framing now explicitly emphasises bytes, and the empirical contribution names two backbones. Introduction and conclusion replace EvaByte's 5.47×/1.22× headline gains with 5.15×/1.17× and add Llama's 2.24× gain over STP.

C2.justification: V2 explains why expressive circuits can help sampling more than greedy decoding and connects EvaByte's strong greedy FF performance to MTP pretraining. It qualifies LoRA benefits by backbone and prior training. A new Limitations section adds substantive discussion of language switching, batch-size applicability and large-vocabulary memory bottlenecks, extending the narrower qualifications in v1.

D1.justification: V1 describes code attached to the submission; v2 supplies a public code/checkpoint location and states that all model variants are released. Appendix E adds target-model architecture and precision details, while Appendices C and F.1 document the FLOP-counting tool and memory-measurement settings. These materially expand reproducibility information, although external availability was not checked.

R1.justification: The extensive related-work taxonomy in v1 Appendix H is replaced by more focused positioning in v2's introduction and Appendix D, explaining the parallel-joint-prediction desiderata and exclusion of Hydra/EAGLE comparisons. V2 also credits Basharin et al. with reporting latency as well as acceptance, correcting v1's acceptance-only characterisation, and adds references on byteification, constrained generation and softmax scalability.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, experimental narrative and conclusion are extensively revised around byte-level prediction, two backbones and decoding-dependent findings. Related-work material is reorganised, a dedicated Limitations section appears, and the appendices gain a substantially different hierarchy. Acceptance terminology and metric explanations are also clarified.

P2.justification: The main paper switches to two columns. Figure 1 is redrawn and relocated, including correction of its latency unit from milliseconds to seconds. Main-text architecture and LoRA comparisons become plots in Figures 3–4, with detailed tables grouped in Appendices K–L. New complexity, model-detail and memory tables and Figures 5–7 substantially expand the presentation; the circuit diagram in Figure 2 is retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence beyond the single MTP-pretrained EvaByte backbone by evaluating byte-level Llama and reporting greedy outcomes that expose limits of expressive heads. Memory analyses, clearer throughput accounting, explicit limitations and code/checkpoint access information improve assessability and reproducibility. Losing RTX 3090 standard deviations is a drawback, and Section 4.3 still overgeneralises CP benefits despite Table 10's contrary greedy EvaByte results. Nevertheless, the broader and better-qualified evidence provides a substantial net improvement.
